text: stillness settled back in across the streets. The wall gave another small creak, the crack widened ever so slightly— —and everything gave way all at once. The boards detonated outward into the playground with a concussive force that scattered every crow on the fence in one explosive black cloud, as a building’s worth of black water tore free from the entranceway and coursed through the grass like a flash flood, churning up gravel and dirt. The school forcefully vomited itself into the playground. Planks cartwheeled across the yard. Plaster chunks hit the asphalt like cannon fire. A locker sailed overhead and buried itself in the fence with a shriek of metal on metal. Ceiling tiles skipped across the flooded grass like thrown stone. Debris churned through the bushes at the yard's edge, shredding leaves and snapping branches, the whole playground receiving everything the building had accumulated over the course of the night in a chaotic surge of flotsam. And among the wreckage, tumbling out in the tide of furniture and broken tile and the last of the flood — Six bodies. David ripped his head free of the water with a strangled gasp. The sound tore out of him raw and violent, barely a breath, more a seizure of the lungs finally allowed to do what they'd been screaming to do for the last sixty seconds. He dragged himself up onto his hands and knees above the receding flood, chest seizing, hacking until bile scorched the back of his throat. His vision pulsed with sparks — the same ones he'd been shaking off for the last four kicks, back with interest now, blotting the edges of everything in slow warning flares. Debris caught against his arms, adding to the small cuts and bruises as he fought to stay somewhat upright and out of the flood. His boots scrabbled uselessly against the flooded grass, the motion still live in his legs long after it had any purpose. His body hadn't gotten the message yet. The momentum still lived in him, still screamed move, survive, break through — the instruction running on without the emergency that had issued it, burning the last of whatever he'd found below exhaustion against ground that didn't need breaking. The tide began to recede just as David’s arms gave out, the school finally finding an end to the flood. He went forward into the churned grass and stayed there, breath hitching and hacking, fingers clawing at the mud like it could tether him to something solid. His whole body trembled, the ache in his limbs blooming hot and bitter, deep and cellular, acid poured straight into his veins. But he could hear them. Around him, near him, the sounds of other people equally wrecked and alive — retching, coughing, tumbling through the debris. He could hear them. He pressed his forehead into the mud and let out a breath that had been waiting a very long time. Thank god. Leon hit the grass rolling, momentum flinging him across the flooded yard in a sodden tumble of limbs. The instinct was faster than thought — knees finding ground, legs pushing, upright before he'd registered that he was out. His eyes were already sweeping the yard, already cataloguing shapes in the debris, already trying to find headcounts through full body coughs that slammed his brain against his skull. His system was filing protests from every direction and he was ignoring every single one of them on the grounds that there wasn't time. The ground tilted sharply under him, his legs buckling against the dizziness. He staggered as the flood tried removing his position, planting a foot wide to catch himself, jaw locked against the grey that was creeping in at the edges of his vision. Not yet. He just needed a second. Just needed to see that they were all— Jake hit him like a sack of wet concrete. Shot out of the flood sideways, completely boneless, no warning, no trajectory that gave Leon any time to brace, Jake's full weight colliding with his legs, making him turn to try and compensate, inevitably taking them both down. Leon went backwards, spine and shoulders catching a discarded locker with a crack that he felt in his back teeth, Jake slamming down alongside him in the receding water, half across his lap, neither of them moving for a moment. The world spun. Kept spinning. Leon's chest heaved, the flood pooling cold around his ankles as if it hadn't finished with him yet, his vision doing something deeply unhelpful at the edges. He tried to push himself upright. His arms had opinions about that. He tried again. His body made the decision for him — just a quiet, final withdrawal of cooperation, the accumulated debt of the last several hours coming due all at once. He felt it happening and couldn't stop it, could only register the specific indignity of going under sitting still, propped against a locker in a puddle, before it took him the rest of the way down. He slumped against the locker with a soft grunt, head tipping to one side as his systems flickered out. The collision knocked something loose in Jake's chest, and he coughed, rough and sputtering, like his body only just remembered how to exist. He hadn't known he needed it to. One moment he was in the dark of the alcove with David’s arm in his grip, and the next Leon's legs were there and the impact drove through him like a starting pistol, his body lurching into function on pure reflex. For a moment, nothing worked right. His chest hitched, trying to summon another round of hacking, the thin thread of air scraping through his throat like broken glass. Not enough. He convulsed once and managed to roll off Leon, collapsing sideways into the muddy grass as his insides revolted. Water. So much water. Too far in, too deep down.
